title: Cornrow Braids Tutorial
metaDescription: How to cornrow hair straight back, beginner-friendly — the flat, close-to-scalp braid technique that works on natural, relaxed and straightened hair alike.

steps.name: Detangle and part
steps.text: Detangle the hair fully, then part off a straight row from the hairline to the nape using the rat-tail comb — a straight, even part is what keeps the finished row looking clean.

steps.name: Start the underhand braid
steps.text: Take a small section at the front of the part and split it into three strands. Cross the outer strands underneath the middle strand (not over) — this is the underhand technique that makes the braid sit flat.

steps.name: Feed in hair as you go
steps.text: With each crossover, pick up a small new section of hair from along the part and add it into the strand before crossing, keeping tension even so the row stays flat against the scalp.

steps.name: Braid to the end
steps.text: Once you reach the nape and there's no more hair to feed in, continue a regular three-strand braid to the ends and secure with a small elastic.

steps.name: Repeat and finish edges
steps.text: Repeat for each row, then smooth the front hairline with a small amount of edge control and a soft-bristle brush.

tips.question: What makes a cornrow lie flat instead of standing up?
tips.answer: Crossing the strands underneath rather than over — that "underhand" motion is the entire difference between a flat cornrow and a raised braid, and it takes practice to get consistent on your own head.

tips.question: Is it possible to cornrow straight, non-textured hair?
tips.answer: Yes, though straight hair has less natural grip, so a small amount of gel or mousse at the root of each row helps the braid hold its shape through the day.

tips.question: How do I keep the parts straight without a mirror behind my head?
tips.answer: A handheld mirror angled against a wall mirror lets you see the back of your part while braiding — doing the first one or two rows slowly and checking often is faster in the long run than redoing a crooked row.

storyIntro: Cornrows are the foundation technique behind most protective styles — Fulani braids, feed-in ponytails and braided updos all start from the same flat, underhand cornrow.

Learning the basic straight-back row first, before attempting a curved or geometric part, is the fastest way to build the muscle memory for tension and feed-in speed that every other cornrow style builds on.
storyNote: Even tension matters more than speed for a first attempt — a slightly loose cornrow can be fixed by redoing one row, but pulling too tight across the whole head can cause real scalp irritation.
